content.text: {"primary_meaning":"Divine judgment upon pervasive human sin and corruption, especially as represented by Noah’s flood; it is commonly paired with God’s preservation of a faithful remnant and the beginning of a renewed creation.","primary_basis":["Genesis 6:5–13 — human wickedness and violence prompt divine judgment.","Genesis 7:17–24 — the flood executes that judgment.","Genesis 8:1–22 — Noah and the creatures are preserved, and the earth is renewed after the waters recede.","Genesis 9:8–17 — God establishes the post-flood covenant and gives the rainbow as its sign.","Matthew 24:37–39 and Luke 17:26–27 — Jesus uses the flood as a pattern of sudden, unexpected judgment.","2 Peter 2:5 and 3:5–7 — the flood is treated as a precedent for judgment upon the ungodly and for future cosmic judgment."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"A type of Christian baptism: passage through judgment-bearing waters into salvation, a cleansed life, or a new beginning.","basis":["1 Peter 3:20–21 explicitly associates the salvation of Noah’s household through water with baptism.","Romans 6:3–4 is sometimes connected conceptually through baptismal death and new life, although it does not mention the flood."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Decreation and re-creation: the floodwaters symbolize a return to primordial chaos, followed by God’s restoration of an ordered world.","basis":["Genesis 1:2, 6–10 provides the creation-water imagery often compared with Genesis 7:11 and 8:1–14.","Genesis 8:1 echoes creation language through God’s wind or Spirit moving over the waters.","Genesis 8–9 presents renewed fertility, human vocation, and covenant after the flood."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"An eschatological pattern foreshadowing the final judgment and the deliverance of God’s people.","basis":["Matthew 24:37–39 and Luke 17:26–30 compare the days of Noah with the coming of the Son of Man.","2 Peter 3:5–7 contrasts the ancient destruction by water with future judgment by fire."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Cleansing or purification of a corrupted earth.","basis":["Genesis 6:11–13 describes the earth as corrupt and filled with violence before the flood.","The removal of the corrupt world and the renewed conditions of Genesis 8–9 support this reading, although Scripture more explicitly emphasizes judgment than ritual cleansing."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The waters of chaos, death, and anti-creation that threaten life but remain subject to God’s sovereignty.","basis":["Genesis 7:11 depicts the release of waters from above and below, reversing the ordered separations of Genesis 1.","Psalm 29:10 and broader biblical water imagery are sometimes read alongside the flood as depictions of God’s rule over overwhelming waters."],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad consensus that the flood’s foremost symbolic or theological Christian interpretation also regularly treats preservation, covenant, new creation, baptism, and final judgment as interconnected secondary meanings rather than mutually exclusive alternatives."}
